messages.content: Defend the thesis that practical knowledge, or knowing how, is not reducible to propositional knowledge, or knowing that. Develop exactly these three claims: (1) Ryle's regress argument shows that if every intelligent performance required first contemplating a proposition, the act of applying that proposition would itself require further propositional knowledge, generating an infinite regress; (2) skilled performance involves context-sensitive responsiveness to particular situations that outstrips any finite set of propositions an agent could articulate or endorse; (3) neuropsychological dissociations, such as amnesic patients who acquire new motor skills while retaining no explicit memory of having practiced them, show that practical and propositional knowledge can come apart. Do not address counterarguments. Write in continuous prose paragraphs only. Do not use bullet points, numbered lists, headers, bold text, or any other formatting.

message.content:
The thesis that practical knowledge cannot be reduced to propositional knowledge finds strong support in several lines of reasoning. Gilbert Ryle's regress argument demonstrates that supposing every intelligent performance depends on first contemplating a proposition leads to an infinite regress, since the application of that proposition would itself demand additional propositional knowledge to guide its proper use. 

Skilled performance requires a context-sensitive responsiveness to the nuances of particular situations, which exceeds what any finite collection of propositions an agent might state or accept could encompass. 

Evidence from neuropsychology reveals dissociations between these forms of knowledge, as seen in amnesic patients who successfully learn new motor skills despite having no explicit recollection of their practice sessions, indicating that practical abilities can develop independently of propositional memory.
message.reasoning:
The task is to defend the thesis that practical knowledge cannot be reduced to propositional knowledge.

The defense will proceed through three arguments. Ryle's regress shows that every intelligent act would require further propositional knowledge, producing an infinite chain. Skilled performance depends on context-sensitive responsiveness that exceeds any finite set of propositions. A third claim is being outlined.

The third argument draws on neuropsychological evidence. Amnesic patients acquire motor skills without retaining explicit memory of practice. This shows practical and propositional knowledge can be severed.

The response will be structured as three flowing paragraphs. The first introduces the thesis and presents Ryle's regress argument.
